source: Google Doc Tab 1 — Kaggle Dataset Test Prompt Suite

batches.name: ieee-fraud
batches.description: IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection (Kaggle competition ieee-fraud-detection) — arc assumes train_transaction.csv (590,540 × 394), train_identity.csv (144,233 × 41), test_transaction.csv, test_identity.csv, sample_submission.csv; target isFraud (~3.5% positive).

items.prompt: I've loaded train_transaction.csv. Before I do anything else, show me the schema — how many columns are there, what are the dtypes, and give me the first 10 rows so I can eyeball it.
Profile this for me. I mainly want the class balance on isFraud and the top 20 columns by missing-value percentage — with 394 columns I need to know what's actually usable.
Run a full profile now. Flag every column that's more than 90% null, and separately tell me which columns are constant or near-constant — I want a drop list before I start modelling.
I'm new to this fraud data. Given what you've seen, what are the three or four analyses you'd run first to figure out what actually separates fraud from legit? Don't run them yet, just tell me.
Remember for this whole project: always report fraud rate as a percentage to 3 decimal places, never drop TransactionID, and treat any column that's >95% null as excluded by default.
Give me fraud rate and mean TransactionAmt broken down by ProductCD, with the transaction count per group, sorted by fraud rate descending.

Join train_transaction.csv to train_identity.csv on TransactionID — left join, I don't want to lose the transactions with no identity record. Then give me fraud rate by DeviceType, and include a bucket for the rows where identity is missing.
TransactionDT is seconds offset from some reference point, not a real timestamp. Derive hour-of-day and day-of-week from it and show me fraud rate by hour — I want to see if fraud clusters overnight.

Bucket TransactionAmt into deciles, then give me fraud rate and row count per decile. Also collapse P_emaildomain — group gmail/yahoo/hotmail/aol/outlook into "free_provider", nulls into "missing", everything else into "other" — and give me fraud rate by that bucket too.
The sample-based numbers won't survive risk review. Re-run fraud rate by card4 and card6 over the entire dataset, not a sample, and confirm in the output which mode you used.
Run a full correlation scan of all the V columns (V1 through V339) against isFraud on the Ray cluster and hand me back the top 25 by absolute correlation. This is too wide to do locally.
This is going to be a recurring workload — spin up a GKE cluster with autoscaling so I can run the wide scans without babysitting my laptop.
Chart it: fraud rate by hour of day as a line chart, and TransactionAmt distribution for fraud vs non-fraud as overlaid histograms on a log x-axis.
Reloading a 590k-row 394-column CSV every session is killing me. Convert train_transaction.csv to Parquet with snappy compression and keep the column names as-is.

Train a binary classifier for isFraud. Features: TransactionAmt, ProductCD, card1, card4, card6, addr1 and C1 through C14. The classes are badly imbalanced so I want precision/recall and AUC, not accuracy. Show me the training plan first — don't run it yet.
Plan looks good but bump it: 30 epochs, learning rate 0.0005, batch size 512, Adam, and run it on two Ray workers. Go ahead and train, then tell me the AUC.
Schedule the fraud-rate-by-ProductCD job to run every 24 hours starting tomorrow morning, give me the task id, and then show me all my scheduled tasks so I can confirm it registered.

batches.name: walmart-sales
batches.description: Walmart Recruiting — Store Sales Forecasting (Kaggle competition walmart-recruiting-store-sales-forecasting) — arc assumes train.csv (421,570 rows), test.csv, features.csv, stores.csv, sampleSubmission.csv; target Weekly_Sales (continuous regression).

items.prompt: Loaded train.csv. Show me the schema and a sample — I want to know the date range covered, how many distinct Store and Dept values there are, and whether the panel is balanced.

Full profile on train.csv. I've noticed Weekly_Sales has negative values — before you flag those as errors, check whether they're plausible returns/markdowns and tell me how many rows and which departments they hit.
Have I looked at Walmart store sales before in this workspace? Pull up whatever prior analysis you have on weekly sales seasonality so I don't redo work.
Total and average Weekly_Sales by Store, plus the number of weeks each store reports. Sort by total descending and show me the top 15.
From Date, derive year, month, ISO week number, and a is_december flag. Then show me average weekly sales by month across all stores — I'm expecting a November/December spike.
For each Store/Dept pair, compute a 4-week trailing average of Weekly_Sales and the year-over-year change versus the same week last year. Return the 20 store/dept pairs with the biggest YoY drop.
The rolling averages need to be right, not approximate — recompute the YoY table over the entire dataset rather than a sample, and tell me explicitly which fidelity mode you ran in.
Run the full store × department × week pivot on the cluster — 421k rows pivoted wide is more than I want to do locally. Give me back the matrix shape and write the result out.
Schedule the store-level weekly rollup to run every Monday at 6am and give me the task id. Then check the status of it.

batches.name: nyc-taxi-duration
batches.description: NYC Taxi Trip Duration (Kaggle competition nyc-taxi-trip-duration) — arc assumes train.csv (1,458,644 rows), test.csv (625,134 rows), sample_submission.csv; target trip_duration (seconds, continuous).

items.prompt: Loaded train.csv — 1.4 million rows. Give me the schema, dtypes, and 10 sample rows. I specifically want to know whether pickup_datetime came in as a string or a real timestamp.
Quick profile. I want min/max/median/p95/p99 on trip_duration and passenger_count, and the value distribution for vendor_id and store_and_fwd_flag.

Full profile with a focus on garbage: how many trips have trip_duration under 60 seconds, over 6 hours, or exactly 86400? And how many have passenger_count of 0? Give me counts and percentages — I want to know what I'm about to throw away.

The goal is predicting trip duration. Talk me through your approach before we build anything — what features would you engineer from raw pickup/dropoff coordinates and timestamps, and what would you exclude?
From here on, always exclude trips shorter than 60 seconds or longer than 6 hours, and drop rows where passenger_count is 0. Apply that filter to everything unless I say otherwise.
Average and median trip_duration by vendor_id and passenger_count, with trip counts. Does vendor 2 genuinely run longer trips or do they just carry more passengers?

Compute haversine distance in kilometres between pickup and dropoff coordinates, then derive average speed in km/h from that and trip_duration. Flag anything over 100 km/h as impossible and tell me how many there are.
From pickup_datetime derive hour, day of week, and month. Then give me a table of average trip duration by hour × day-of-week — I'm looking for the rush hour signature.

Round pickup lat/lon to 3 decimal places to make a grid, then give me the top 20 pickup cells by trip volume with their average duration. Label them by neighbourhood if you can infer it from the coordinates.
Rerun the hour × day-of-week duration table across all 1.46 million rows, not a sample — I need the real numbers for the ops deck. Confirm which fidelity mode you used.
Run the full haversine + speed computation over the entire file on the Ray cluster and write the enriched dataset out. This is the one I'll be modelling on.
Chart the demand pattern: trips per hour of day as a line, and a 2D density heatmap of pickup locations over Manhattan.
Convert the enriched dataset to Parquet partitioned by pickup month. The raw CSV parse is the slowest part of my loop.

Build a regression model for trip_duration. Features: haversine distance, passenger_count, vendor_id, pickup hour, pickup day of week, and store_and_fwd_flag. Predict on log1p of duration since it's heavily right-skewed. And do not use dropoff_datetime — it isn't in the test set. Show me the plan first.
items.purpose: Model training (plan generation + leakage guard) — train.csv

items.prompt: Run that training on Ray with 4 workers, 40 epochs, learning rate 0.001, batch size 1024. Report RMSLE on the holdout.

batches.name: instacart
batches.description: Instacart Market Basket Analysis (Kaggle competition instacart-market-basket-analysis) — arc assumes orders.csv (3.4M rows), order_products__prior.csv (32.4M rows), order_products__train.csv (1.38M rows), products.csv (49,688 rows), aisles.csv (134 rows), departments.csv (21 rows), sample_submission.csv; target reordered (binary).

items.prompt: Full profile on orders.csv. days_since_prior_order has nulls — check whether they line up exactly with order_number = 1. If they do, that's structural, don't tell me to impute it. Also give me the eval_set split.
Note for this project: I only care about departments with more than 100,000 order lines, and always show product names rather than raw product_id. Apply that everywhere.
Register my Postgres warehouse as a connection so I can push results there, then list everything I've got connected.

caveats: Connection aliases must be registered (UI: Cloud Datasets / Databases) before the data-transfer prompts, or swapped for existing names: analytics_lake = GCS or S3 bucket connection (write access); analytics_warehouse = Postgres or MySQL connection (write access); s3_archive = a second cloud bucket connection, ideally a different provider than analytics_lake — that difference is what makes the cross-cloud path real.

Ordering (doc §1.3): prompts are stateful within a dataset — run each batch's 20 prompts in order, in one session. Slots 15–20 in particular depend on earlier turns: DTA prompts assume a transformed result exists (the DTA treats the active dataset as the implicit source); inference (slot 19) assumes training (17–18) completed and a model is registered; scheduling (slot 20) assumes a generated job exists to schedule.

depends_on_prior encoding: true for all slots 15–20 per §1.3's blanket rule, plus earlier slots whose text references an artifact built in a prior turn (ieee-fraud 13 'Chart it'; walmart-sales 10 'the YoY table', 13, 14 'the joined table'; nyc-taxi-duration 11 'the hour × day-of-week table', 12 'the full haversine + speed computation', 13, 14 'the enriched dataset'; instacart 11 'the association rules', 12 'the full user-feature build', 14 'Visualise it'). Some true-marked slots are nevertheless self-contained in wording (e.g., nyc-taxi-duration 17, instacart 15).
Purpose field encodes two doc columns as '<Testing part> — <Data file name>'; '(session-level)' / '(cluster-level)' are the doc's own file-column values for non-file-scoped prompts.

Pass criteria (doc §1.4): for each prompt record (a) which planner tool was called, (b) which graph node executed, (c) whether generated code passed all three validators, (d) whether the numeric answer is correct — a plausible-looking wrong number is a failure, not a pass.

Kaggle setup (doc §1.1): all four are competition datasets (kaggle competitions download, not datasets); each requires accepting the competition rules on the Kaggle site once. Walmart ships .csv.zip members inside the outer zip (needs a second unzip pass); Instacart ships a nested instacart_2017_05_01/ folder (flatten it or point Avaloka at the nested path). The repo helper tests/download_kaggle_datasets.py will not fetch these four.

Coverage gaps (doc §7): EKS provisioning untested (only GKE, ieee-fraud 12 — duplicate with AWS wording against Walmart); cross-cloud C2C only real if s3_archive (walmart-sales 15) is on a different provider than analytics_lake — worth an explicit GCS→S3 prompt; only CSV→Parquet DTA format exercised (Avro, Delta, Iceberg, XML, Excel untested — repeat slot-14-style prompts with other target formats); no validator failure paths (all prompts well-formed — add deliberately broken prompts: nonexistent column, impossible join key, ambiguous target).

Suggested execution order (doc §8), escalating cost/infra: (1) prompts 1–10 all datasets, local only; (2) fidelity + distributed 10–12 (needs Ray; nyc-taxi and instacart are the ones big enough to show the difference); (3) cloud transfer 14–17 (needs the three connections registered); (4) training + inference 17–20 (IEEE first — imbalanced binary classification is the harshest metric test); (5) scheduling 20 (needs Celery worker and Redis up).

Pruned 32 items referencing files/connections absent from the test bucket (v1 was written vs public Kaggle schemas: walmart-recruiting features.csv/stores.csv, instacart order_products__*, and alias connections analytics_lake/warehouse/s3_archive). Remaining items use only files present in the bucket.
